## Chapter 38: Control

### Revisiting the FMEA and Closing the Loop with the Control Plan

At the end of the improve phase and the start of the control phase, Six Sigma teams revisit the FMEA created in the measure phase (Chapter 35), logging which actions were completed and reassessing each row's SEV, OCC, DET, and Action Priority in light of the improved process. For any root cause that was addressed, the team expects to see Occurrence or Detection improve — and, when the cause was eliminated, the Action Priority drop to Low.

The revised FMEA doesn't stand alone: it feeds directly into the Control Plan. Every prevention or detection control listed in the FMEA to reduce OCC or DET should show up as a monitored item in the Control Plan, with a defined measurement method, frequency, and acceptance criterion. This forms a traceable chain:

**FMEA** (risks and controls) → **Control Plan** (formalized controls) → **MSA** (confidence in the control's measurement) → **SPC** (ongoing stability monitoring) → **reaction** (corrective action when the process signals a deviation)

Revisiting the FMEA at this point serves two purposes. First, it documents the real gain achieved from the solutions implemented. Second — and this is where continuous improvement actually happens — it identifies which potential failure now carries the highest priority now that the previous one has been addressed, pointing to the next improvement target. Control isn't the end of the cycle; it's the moment to make sure the gain holds and to point toward where to continue.

### Creating a Control Plan

To help sustain ongoing success, Six Sigma teams should create a written control plan for the process owner. The purpose of a control plan is to help the process owner and business team track and respond to key performance indicators, so the process stays improved. The control plan should be a concise, easy-to-reference document that tells the business team when to monitor, how to monitor, what range of data is acceptable in monitoring, and how to respond with corrective action if the measured range isn't acceptable.

Control plans can be spreadsheets, specialized digital documents, or printed documents posted at a workstation. Common elements of a control plan include:

- Company, division, or department name
- Name of the person who created the plan
- Date the plan was created
- Name of the person who last edited the plan
- Date the plan was last edited
- Project and/or process name or identifier
- Process owner
- List of process steps where control action is needed
- CTQ or metric associated with each required action
- Limit specifications, or the acceptable measurement range
- The unit of measurement
- The measurement method
- The required sample size
- The measurement frequency
- The person responsible for measurement
- Where the information is logged
- Corrective actions
- Associated policy and procedure documents

When discussing quality in Chapter 6, we introduced the example of a company that makes chocolate bars and noted that the amount of sugar in the chocolate bar recipe was critical to the customer's experience with the finished product. If a Six Sigma team were tasked with improving customer satisfaction with a new chocolate-bar product, it might have implemented a solution that ensures the correct amount of sugar gets added to the mix at the right temperature, to properly incorporate the ingredient.

A control plan for the new chocolate-bar solution might look like the document below.

*(LSL = Lower Specification Limit, USL = Upper Specification Limit)*

The control plan example above provides instructions for two specific process steps, with easy-to-understand measurement and monitoring requirements. To reduce the chance of errors, the Six Sigma team even specified a special measurement tool for measuring the sugar in the test batch, so every operator doing the monitoring measures using the same tool.

At the end of the control document, the team provides steps for corrective action. The first step can be corrected by the operator themselves, who has the ability to calibrate the machine alone. Temperature calibration, in this case, can't be performed by the operator, which means the process needs to be halted, so someone can address the issue. Note that it's always preferable, when possible, to build the corrective action at the process level, as was done with the sugar measurement. This minimizes downtime, puts employees more in control of the processes they own, and helps employees stay engaged with the quality process.

The control plan above assumes measurements need to be taken or logged manually. Ideally, Six Sigma teams should look for ways to automate measurements, which means data can be collected continuously and converted into statistical process controls, like control charts. Automated data collection doesn't mean a control plan isn't needed, it just means a control plan won't include instructions for collecting the data. Instead, employees and process owners can be instructed to review automated data or control charts and act if needed.

You'll also notice the specification requirements provided above come with LSL and USL. LSL is the lower specification limit, and USL is the upper specification limit. These are the upper and lower bounds of the acceptable range.

### Visual Management

Beyond providing a control plan, Six Sigma teams can implement specific visual controls in a work environment, to help business teams keep a process under control. Some of these tools were covered in Chapter 18, on Lean process management, including 5S. Other visual controls teams can implement include posted signs, matrices, and instructions, audit boards that let teams track individual or group performance over time, color coding, and safety signage.

Standard operating procedures can often be distilled into visual poster representations. A coffee shop, for example, might give employees a visual representation of the ingredients used to create various complex drink flavors. Such a poster ensures employees can prepare drinks quickly, reducing errors in ingredient inclusion.

Other SOP visualizations can include safety procedures in a medical setting, like visual reminders for handwashing and small pictorial representations of how to operate equipment, like hospital beds. In an office setting, pictorial instructions are found on copy machines, where images indicate how paper should be loaded, and visual gifs are often displayed on LED screens to help employees clear paper jams. These are a few examples Six Sigma teams can follow when creating documents that'll help the business team take ownership of an improved process and sustain the improvements made.

### Statistical Process Control (SPC) Charts

One of the most common methods Six Sigma teams use to monitor a process is the control chart. There are several types of control charts, and Six Sigma specialists need to choose the right control chart for the data type and analytical purpose.

Now, let's cover the visual tests that let a Six Sigma team or process owner know a process is out of control.

A basic control chart has the following elements:

- A data line chart, with points plotted for specific data points
- An x-bar line, representing the mean of the data points
- Lines above and below the x-bar line, representing 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations from the mean, in each direction
- An upper control limit (UCL) line at 3 standard deviations above the mean
- A lower control limit (LCL) line at 3 standard deviations below the mean

<img alt="Gráfico de controle de exemplo: linha central (x-barra) em preto, limites de 1 e 2 desvios padrão em verde, limites superior e inferior de controle em laranja, com zonas A, B, e C marcadas em ambos os lados" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


Above is an example of a control chart. The middle line, which is black, is the x-bar line. The x-bar line is bounded by green lines on either side, indicating 1 and 2 standard deviations away from the center line. Those lines are bounded by orange lines on each side: at the top, the upper control limit, and at the bottom, the lower control limit. Between the various lines are areas of the control chart, designated as C, B, and A, in each direction. These distinct areas are important for understanding whether a process might be out of control. They're also called Zones 1, 2, and 3.

A control chart is best displayed using an automated reporting system or dashboard, where process owners or responsible employees can view it as needed. If automated data collection and control chart creation aren't possible, then a business analyst may be tasked with collecting data and presenting it in this format periodically, though periodic graphical analysis is less likely to catch a control problem within a process.

#### Statistical Process Control Tests: Control Charts

There are eight tests that can quickly tell whoever is watching a control chart whether a process is out of control.

- **Test one:** A single point on the control chart appears outside the upper or lower control limits. If this happens, process owners should take immediate action, because it's evidence of a major problem within a process. Although there's a very remote possibility that deviations beyond three standard deviations occur randomly, the probability is only 3 in 1,000.
- **Test two:** Nine points in a row appear on one side of the center line. This indicates a shift occurred in the process; if the process owner knows what change caused the shift and it was intentional, nothing needs to be done, and the control chart will adjust itself over time, with the new data. Otherwise, the process owner should investigate the process.
- **Test three:** Six points on the control chart increase or decrease in sequence, indicating the process is becoming less or more efficient, or is generating fewer or more errors. Process owners should investigate, unless there's a known reason for the trend.
- **Test four:** Fourteen points on the control chart, in sequence, alternate going up and down. This can indicate variation in machines, employees, shifts, or overcorrection.
- **Test five:** Two of three points in a row on the control chart are in the upper A section or the lower A section. This can indicate some kind of special cause, creating sudden high variation.
- **Test six:** Four of five points in a row on the control chart are located in the upper B section (or beyond) or the lower B section (or beyond). This can indicate a larger cause issue, or a shift problem similar to test four.
- **Test seven:** Fifteen points in a row are located within the C section, above or below the center line. This can indicate the control limits are no longer relevant for the process; if a team improved a process's variation, it should recalculate the control limits for the new parameters. Alternatively, this can happen temporarily when short-term variation is high or low relative to the rest of the points on a control chart.
- **Test eight:** Eight points in a row on the control chart are located on either side of the center line, but none is located in the C section, above or below the line. This can indicate a resource issue or mixed processes; a team might find it's measuring a single process when it's actually measuring two processes, for example. Alternatively, it can indicate a big difference in processing between two employees or teams.

When it's possible to create control charts and display current data regularly, these charts are a good addition to a control plan. Individuals don't need to be well-versed in statistical process control to learn about the eight tests, and business teams that benefit from control charts can spend more time working on production or fixing problems, and less time collecting and documenting measurements.

#### Worked example across five approaches: automatic detection of 2 of the 8 tests

The text above describes the 8 visual tests conceptually. Here we automate detection of **Test one** (point beyond UCL/LCL) and **Test two** (9 points in a row on the same side of the center line) over an **illustrative** series of 20 subgroup means: the first 10 points form the baseline (used to fix the center line and limits); the 11th point is an isolated deviation; the last 9 stay consistently above the center line.

`Baseline: 48, 52, 49, 51, 50, 48, 52, 49, 51, 50`

`Full sequence: [baseline] + 61, 51, 52, 53, 52, 53, 52, 54, 53, 54`

The cross-references cover the rest: Test three (trend), Test four (zigzag), and the zone tests (five through eight) use the same sliding-window logic over the A/B/C zones — Chapter 67 (PART V) revisits this same set of tests, already built natively into Minitab.

<img alt="Ilustracao Excel + Power BI (DAX) do exemplo: detecção automática de 2 dos 8 testes" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," style="max-width:100%;" />

**Excel 365**: with the data in A1:A20, the center line in a named cell `CL` (`=AVERAGE(A1:A10)`) and the baseline standard deviation in `SD` (`=STDEV.S(A1:A10)`), calculate `UCL=CL+3*SD` and `LCL=CL-3*SD`. **Test one** is a direct formula: `=OR(A1>UCL, A1<LCL)`. **Test two** requires a sliding window: `=SUMPRODUCT(--(OFFSET(A1,0,0,9,1)>CL))=9` (all 9 points in the window above the center line) added to the equivalent for "below," dragged cell by cell — it works, but it gets unreadable fast for the larger window tests (14 or 15 points); it's exactly this kind of formula that makes Minitab/R worth using when the control plan depends on the 8 tests.

**Power BI (DAX)**: **Test one** is native and direct (a simple comparison of a measure against limits). The sequence/window tests (two through eight) depend on window functions (`OFFSET`/`WINDOW`, available in the most recent DAX versions) and get impractical to maintain — the recommended pattern is to calculate the 8 tests in Python/R/Minitab and publish the violations as a table imported into Power BI to flag on the dashboard:

```dax
Teste 1 - Fora dos Limites =
IF ( [Valor Medido] > [UCL] || [Valor Medido] < [LCL], "Violação", "OK" )
```

```py-r
--- python
import numpy as np

linha_base = [48, 52, 49, 51, 50, 48, 52, 49, 51, 50]
serie = linha_base + [61, 51, 52, 53, 52, 53, 52, 54, 53, 54]
serie = np.array(serie)

linha_central = np.mean(linha_base)
sigma = np.std(linha_base, ddof=1)
ucl, lcl = linha_central + 3*sigma, linha_central - 3*sigma
print(f"Linha central={linha_central:.2f}  sigma={sigma:.3f}  UCL={ucl:.2f}  LCL={lcl:.2f}")

teste1 = np.where((serie > ucl) | (serie < lcl))[0] + 1
print("Teste um (ponto além dos limites), posições:", list(teste1))

sinais = np.where(serie > linha_central, 1, np.where(serie < linha_central, -1, 0))
janelas_teste2 = [
    (i+1, i+9) for i in range(len(sinais)-8)
    if all(sinais[i:i+9] == 1) or all(sinais[i:i+9] == -1)
]
print("Teste dois (9 pontos seguidos do mesmo lado), janelas:", janelas_teste2)
```

```py-r
--- python
%%R
linha_base <- c(48, 52, 49, 51, 50, 48, 52, 49, 51, 50)
serie <- c(linha_base, 61, 51, 52, 53, 52, 53, 52, 54, 53, 54)

linha_central <- mean(linha_base)
sigma <- sd(linha_base)
ucl <- linha_central + 3*sigma
lcl <- linha_central - 3*sigma
cat(sprintf("Linha central=%.2f sigma=%.3f UCL=%.2f LCL=%.2f\n", linha_central, sigma, ucl, lcl))

teste1 <- which(serie > ucl | serie < lcl)
cat("Teste um, posicoes:", teste1, "\n")

sinais <- ifelse(serie > linha_central, 1, ifelse(serie < linha_central, -1, 0))
for (i in 1:(length(sinais)-8)) {
  janela <- sinais[i:(i+8)]
  if (all(janela == 1) || all(janela == -1)) {
    cat(sprintf("Teste dois, janela %d-%d\n", i, i+8))
  }
}
```

**Minitab** (current version — check minitab.com): with the data in C1, go to **Stat → Control Charts → Variables Charts for Individuals → Individuals** (or **Xbar-R** if the data comes in subgroups), and under **I Chart Options → Tests**, select *Perform all tests for special causes*. Minitab applies the 8 tests described in the text automatically and marks on the chart which point violates which test — the same 1-through-8 numbering from the manual.

*Verification note: Python and R agree exactly — center line=50.00, UCL≈54.47, LCL≈45.53; point 11 (value 61) violates Test one; points 12–20 form a window of 9 in a row above the center line, violating Test two. Excel, DAX, and Minitab are checked manually against these positions.*

### Control Versus Capability

It's important to note the distinction between a process that's under control and one that's capable of meeting customer requirements. We touched on this concept in PART I: controlled processes don't have much variation. Capable processes don't have much variation, and the outputs are centered around a customer requirement. That's why both control limits and specification limits matter.

Consider the example used earlier in this chapter about the sugar in the chocolate mix. The specification limits ranged from 4.9 to 5.1 cups of sugar in each batch. It's possible for a control chart to show the process is under control, if measurements range from 3.5 to 3.6 cups of sugar per batch, but the process owner should know those measurements won't contribute to a product that meets customer-critical quality requirements.

To understand how a process is performing relative to the specification limits, Six Sigma teams can calculate the sigma level and process capability.

**Sigma Level**

The sigma level is the number of standard deviations between the process's current center, measured by the mean, and the nearest specification limit (not the control limit). The equation for the sigma level is the smaller of the following calculations:

**(USL − x̄) / σ or (LSL − x̄) / σ**

For example, if a process has a USL of 5 and an LSL of 3, a standard deviation of 0.25, and a mean of 4.2, then you'd calculate from the USL, since the mean is closer to the USL.

(5 − 4.2) / 0.25 = 3.2 = sigma level

**Process Capability**

Process capability is calculated by dividing the sigma level by 3. In the example's case, the capability is 1.06.

Process capability is denoted as Cpk. A process capability of 1.33 equals a sigma level of 4, which most specialists agree is the minimum level at which most customers will be satisfied. Under statistical process control, many organizations aim for a process capability of 2.0, with minimally acceptable process capability at 1.5.

### Team Celebration and Reflection

When Six Sigma teams consider the improvements and the related process capable and under control, and have already handed those processes back to the business's and process owner's control, they should set aside time to celebrate and reflect on the project's outcome. This is generally done after the final tollgate review with a sponsor or champion, and can be a quick meeting to tie up loose ends, recognize the work done by the team, and discuss lessons learned within the process.

The celebration-and-reflection meeting is also a great time for team members to bring up ideas for possible future improvement projects. While the improvements — and the related problems and causes — are still fresh in the team's mind, they can brainstorm effectively about ideas for next steps. As with any brainstorming session, no idea should be automatically dismissed for seeming silly, being too hard to implement, being too expensive, or seeming too big. Not every idea will become a future project, but the team's input provides valuable information the Black Belt can later share with Six Sigma leadership boards.

### Control Tollgate Checklist

- The team calculated the new process's performance and capability.
- The team wrote a control plan and communicated it to the process owner.
- The team built a monitor for the process, whether through manual data-collection procedures or automated control-chart generation.
- The team provided the process owner and business team with every tool and piece of information needed to sustain the improvements.
- The sponsor, champion, or executive leadership was informed about the state of the improvements.
- The team met to reflect on the project and generate a list of ideas for future improvements.
